title: Imitation and the limits of resemblance
content: The oldest account of artistic value holds that a painting succeeds insofar as it resembles what it depicts. This assumption governed European criticism for centuries, and it retains an intuitive appeal, because resemblance seems measurable in a way that expression does not. Yet the criterion collapses under examination. A portrait resembles its subject far less than a photograph does, and a photograph resembles its subject far less than a mirror does; nevertheless nobody considers mirrors the supreme achievement of representational art. Resemblance, moreover, is symmetrical, whereas depiction is not. If a canvas resembles a landscape, then the landscape resembles the canvas equally, and yet the landscape does not depict anything at all. The difficulty deepens when we notice that resemblance is always resemblance in some respect. Everything resembles everything else in indefinitely many respects, so the criterion tells us nothing until we specify which respects matter, and that specification is precisely what a theory of depiction was supposed to supply. Philosophers of art therefore replaced resemblance with convention, arguing that pictures denote in the manner of symbols rather than mirrors. On this account a painting refers to its subject because a community has established the practice of taking it so, much as a word refers to its object without sounding like it. Such conventionalism explains why unfamiliar pictorial systems appear illegible to viewers trained in another tradition, and why perspective, once thought to record vision faithfully, is now understood as a learned notation. The consequence is unsettling for anyone who wanted an objective standard. If depiction rests on convention, then the apparent naturalness of realistic painting is an artifact of habit, and the styles we call distorted are simply those whose conventions we have not internalized. Realism becomes a historical achievement rather than a natural baseline, and the question of artistic value must be answered on other grounds entirely.

title: Why performance resists preservation
content: A novel survives its author because the marks on the page carry everything essential to the work. A symphony survives because notation preserves the relations among pitches and durations that constitute the composition. Performance art enjoys no such security. What a dancer accomplishes exists only during the interval of its accomplishment, and the documentation that remains afterward stands to the performance roughly as a photograph of a meal stands to its taste. This disparity has consequences that extend well beyond archival inconvenience. Because performance cannot be stored, it cannot easily be bought, sold, or accumulated, and consequently it occupies an awkward position within institutions organized around permanent collections. Museums acquire objects; they cannot acquire an afternoon. Curators have responded by purchasing instructions rather than events, treating the choreographer's directions as the enduring work and each realization as a mere instance. Yet this solution imports the very assumption it was meant to avoid, since it relocates the artwork into a durable text and thereby denies that the transient encounter was the point. Some theorists accept the loss and argue that impermanence constitutes the meaning of the form. On their view a performance criticizes the acquisitive logic of the art market precisely by refusing to leave anything behind, and any attempt at preservation betrays it. Others reply that this romanticizes disappearance and consigns whole traditions to oblivion, particularly those of communities whose practices were never written down. The dispute is not merely academic, because it determines which histories can be told. Where documentation is dismissed as inauthentic, the record thins, and later generations inherit an account assembled from whatever happened to be durable. Impermanence, in other words, is never neutral; it distributes forgetting unevenly, and it does so along lines that follow existing inequalities of attention and resources rather than any principle internal to the art itself.

title: Ornament, function, and the moral rhetoric of design
content: Early modern architects argued that decoration was not merely superfluous but dishonest, since it concealed the structure that actually held a building up. Their polemic identified ornament with deception and stripped surfaces with integrity, and this equation proved remarkably persuasive, shaping a century of construction. Nevertheless the argument rests on an assumption that deserves scrutiny, namely that a building has a single truth which its surface either reveals or hides. Structures are not transparent in that manner. A steel frame is already invisible beneath its cladding, and the smooth concrete plane that supposedly expresses honesty is itself a finish applied over reinforcement. What the reformers offered was therefore not the absence of rhetoric but a different rhetoric, one whose vocabulary happened to consist of plainness rather than foliage. Anthropologists studying craft traditions elsewhere reach a similar conclusion from another direction. In many societies the decorated surface carries information that the object could not otherwise convey, recording lineage, rank, or obligation in patterns that members of the community read fluently. To call such patterns superfluous is to mistake unfamiliarity for meaninglessness, because the observer who cannot read them perceives only excess where participants perceive a statement. Ornament, on this account, is a medium rather than a residue, and its removal deletes content instead of clarifying it. The modern preference for undecorated form thus appears less as a discovery about buildings than as a claim about which kinds of meaning deserve to be visible. Once the claim is recognized as a claim, the moral vocabulary that surrounded it becomes difficult to sustain. Honesty and deception are the wrong terms for a choice between competing conventions, and the question returns to where it belongs: what a given community wants its surroundings to say, and to whom.

title: The invention of the audience
content: Silence in the concert hall feels like an obvious expression of respect, but it is a comparatively recent arrangement. Through much of the eighteenth century listeners conversed, ate, arrived late, and applauded between movements, and performers expected as much. The transformation into an immobile and quiet public occurred gradually, and it accompanied changes that had little to do with music itself. Halls grew larger and darker, tickets were sold to strangers rather than distributed within a court, and the printed program appeared to tell newcomers what they were hearing. Each of these developments encouraged a particular posture, and together they produced the modern audience as we recognize it. What deserves attention is how thoroughly the arrangement came to seem natural. Contemporary listeners experience a cough as an intrusion and a phone as a violation, which indicates that the convention now carries moral weight rather than mere etiquette. Historians of the concert therefore treat attention itself as an artifact with a history, shaped by architecture, commerce, and the ambitions of composers who wanted their structures grasped whole. Such an approach has consequences for how we evaluate other listening practices. If concentrated silence is a convention rather than the natural response to serious music, then background listening is not obviously a degradation, and the traditions in which music accompanies work or worship are not deficient versions of the concert. They are alternative arrangements with their own demands. The point is not that all arrangements are equivalent, since each makes certain features audible and others inaudible. It is rather that the concert hall cannot serve as the standard against which the rest are measured, because it is one historical solution among several to the problem of how a group of people should attend to sound together.

title: Authenticity and the copy
content: A forgery may be indistinguishable from an original under any examination available to the eye, and yet its discovery transforms our estimation of it completely. This reaction puzzles philosophers, because if the visible properties are identical, the aesthetic experience should be identical as well. Something other than appearance is evidently doing the work. One explanation locates the difference in history rather than surface. An original stands in a particular causal relation to its maker, and that relation constitutes part of what we value, much as a letter from a friend differs from a perfect facsimile despite identical wording. On this account authenticity is not a perceptible quality but a fact about origin, and our response tracks the fact rather than the appearance. A second explanation is less metaphysical. Knowing that a work is a forgery changes what we look for, and therefore changes what we see. The connoisseur who learns of the deception begins to notice hesitations in the brushwork that previously read as confidence, because expectation shapes perception in ways that introspection does not reveal. Neither explanation is complete on its own. The historical account cannot explain why forgeries sometimes withstand scrutiny for decades, and the perceptual account cannot explain why our estimation drops even when no new visual difference is ever found. What both make clear, however, is that aesthetic judgment is not confined to the surface presented to the eye. It draws on beliefs about how the object came to exist, and those beliefs are revisable. Consequently the value of a work is never fixed by its appearance alone, and the discovery of a document in an archive can alter a painting that has not changed in any physical respect whatsoever.

title: Museums and the problem of context
content: An object placed in a gallery acquires properties it did not previously possess. A mask carved for a ceremony becomes a sculpture; a reliquary becomes an example of metalwork; a chair becomes a document of design history. The transformation is accomplished by the room rather than by anything done to the object, and it is largely invisible to visitors, who experience the resulting arrangement as a neutral presentation of things that speak for themselves. Curators have long recognized this difficulty and have attempted various remedies. Period rooms reconstruct an original setting, wall texts supply the missing occasion, and recorded voices describe the practices in which the object once participated. Each remedy, however, introduces its own frame. The period room is itself a nineteenth-century invention that arranges the past according to modern notions of domestic coherence, and the explanatory label speaks in an institutional voice that positions the visitor as a student rather than a participant. Context, in other words, cannot be restored; it can only be replaced with another context whose constructedness is easier to overlook. This does not render the enterprise futile, but it changes what honesty requires. Instead of promising an unmediated encounter, an exhibition can make its own choices visible, showing how the object arrived, who decided what to display, and what was left in storage. Such disclosure will not return the mask to the ceremony, and it may disappoint visitors who came for the reassuring impression of direct contact with another world. Yet it offers something the reassuring version cannot, namely an accurate picture of what a museum is: not a window onto other cultures but an institution that assembles fragments and arranges them according to purposes of its own.

title: Improvisation and the myth of spontaneity
content: Listeners often describe improvisation as the absence of preparation, as though the performer had invented everything at the moment of playing. Musicians who improvise describe their practice quite differently. They speak of vocabularies accumulated over years, of phrases rehearsed until they are available without deliberation, and of harmonic frameworks so thoroughly internalized that the player can attend to shape rather than to mechanics. Spontaneity, on this account, is not the opposite of preparation but its product, since only extensive preparation makes rapid choice possible. The distinction matters because the popular picture assigns improvisation to inspiration and composition to labor, and this division has consequences for how traditions are valued. Musical cultures whose repertoire is transmitted by ear rather than in notation have frequently been described as instinctive, and the description, though intended as praise, denies them the credit given to written traditions for craft and deliberation. What appears effortless is thereby mistaken for what required no effort. Research on expertise supports the performers rather than the listeners. Skilled improvisers show the same reliance on stored patterns that chess masters display when they recognize a position, and their fluency comes from retrieval rather than invention. The freedom that audiences hear is real, but it is freedom within a structure that constrains most possibilities in advance, leaving a manageable set among which the player chooses. Recognizing this does not diminish the achievement. It relocates the achievement to where practitioners have always placed it, in the long accumulation of resources that makes a decision possible in the space of a beat, and it removes the condescension that follows whenever skill is redescribed as instinct.

title: Translation and the untranslatable
content: Every translator confronts passages that appear to resist transfer entirely: a pun whose two meanings have no common equivalent, a form of address that encodes a social relation the target language does not mark, a rhythm inseparable from the sounds that carry it. The traditional response treats such moments as losses to be minimized, and the translator's task as the recovery of as much as circumstances permit. A different tradition regards them as the most instructive part of the work. On this view the untranslatable is not a defect in the target language but evidence about the source, because the resistance reveals what a language obliges its speakers to specify. A tongue that distinguishes several degrees of formality compels a choice that another leaves open, and the translator who must select among options discovers a structure that native readers never notice. Difficulty thus becomes a method of description rather than an obstacle to it. This reframing changes the standard by which translations are judged. If fidelity means producing the same effect, then the translator may legitimately depart from the words, replacing a pun with a different pun and a meter with a different meter. If fidelity means preserving the strangeness, then the translation should retain what the target language finds awkward, allowing readers to feel the shape of a system unlike their own. The two ideals cannot be satisfied simultaneously, and the choice between them is not technical but interpretive. It reflects a judgment about what readers are owed: a text that reads as though it had been written for them, or a text that reminds them continually that it was not.

title: Taste, distinction, and the sociology of preference
content: Preferences in music, food, and furnishing feel intensely personal, and people commonly defend them as expressions of individual sensibility. Sociological research complicates this account without quite refuting it. Large surveys find that taste correlates strongly with education and upbringing, and that the correlations persist after income is held constant, which suggests that what people enjoy is bound up with how they were formed rather than with what they can afford. The mechanism proposed is dispositional rather than deliberate. Children acquire habits of attention from the households in which they grow up, learning which objects reward close inspection and which conversations count as serious, and these habits later present themselves as preferences that seem to arise from nowhere. Because the acquisition is early and largely unremarked, its results feel natural, and their social origin is invisible precisely to those who possess them. Critics of this framework observe that it explains too much. If every preference expresses a position in a social structure, then the account cannot distinguish between a judgment reached through sustained attention and one absorbed unreflectively, and it leaves no room for anyone to change their mind on the merits. Defenders reply that the framework describes tendencies rather than destinies, and that showing an origin does not settle the question of validity. The unresolved dispute nevertheless leaves something established. Whatever else taste may be, it is not innocent of history, and the confidence with which people report their preferences is a poor guide to where those preferences came from.

title: Ritual, repetition, and the making of meaning
content: Anthropologists once explained ritual as a means of expressing beliefs that participants already held, treating the ceremony as an outward sign of an inward conviction. Extended fieldwork made this account difficult to sustain. Participants frequently disagreed about what a rite meant, offered explanations that contradicted one another, or declined to interpret it at all, insisting instead that the actions were correct and that correctness was the point. Belief, it appeared, was not what the ritual expressed but something the observer had supplied. An alternative account reverses the relation. On this view repeated action does not follow from conviction; it produces the dispositions from which conviction later emerges. Standing, kneeling, and reciting in unison establish a bodily habit of participation, and the sense of significance attaches afterward to whatever the community offers as explanation. The absence of shared interpretation therefore ceases to be puzzling, because agreement was never located in the interpretations. It was located in the practice. This reversal has implications well beyond religion. Institutions of every kind rely on repeated forms whose participants could not readily justify them, from the procedures of a court to the conventions of an academic seminar, and in each case the form does work that no statement of purpose could accomplish. Attempts at reform that address only the stated rationale consequently tend to fail, because they leave the practice intact and the practice was doing the work. Understanding this does not make ritual immune to criticism. It does suggest that criticism aimed at the beliefs of participants often misses its target, since the beliefs are downstream of the actions rather than their source.
